summary: Each layer has an incumbent. Binary composition analysis (Synopsys/Codenomicon AppCheck, Black Duck) and the binwalk maintainers' own commercial firmware scanner cover analysis. UL 2900 / CAP and ICSA-style labs own certification trust, and chip vendors push their own schemes. Open space remains in device-specific requirements plus remediation guidance for makers without security teams. Certification is the weakest claim.

objections.objection: Most dangerous competitor: UL (with peer labs such as ICSA Labs, TUV). UL already runs a cybersecurity assurance program built on the UL 2900 standard for network-connectable products, and its test process uses automated binary/composition scanning alongside manual testing. Buyers, carriers and regulators recognise a UL mark. A startup's certificate has no such standing, and UL can add more automation and cheaper tiers faster than a startup can earn recognition. The concept itself admits the certification needs a recognised standard.
objections.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UL_(safety_organization) (UL 2900-1 Software Cybersecurity for Network-Connectable Products); concept:risks (Certification without a recognised standard has limited weight; Large testing labs adopt automation); concept:build.hardest_parts

objections.objection: Firmware binary analysis is already commercial and being bundled into SCA suites. Synopsys (which bought Codenomicon and its AppCheck/Protecode binary scanner, then Black Duck in 2017) sells upload-a-binary component and CVE analysis to the same embedded makers through existing AppSec relationships. The binwalk maintainers (ReFirm Labs) and Finite State are turning automated firmware analysis into products. 'Upload firmware, get exposures' is a feature, not a differentiator.
objections.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Duck_Software (acquired by Synopsys 2017, combined into Software Integrity Group); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codenomicon; concept:competitors (binwalk url github.com/ReFirmLabs/binwalk, Finite State)

objections.objection: Free and open-source substitutes cover much of the analysis wedge: binwalk, firmadyne, FKIE's FACT firmware analysis framework, and cheap CVE lookups. The planned free report wedge competes with free tools makers' engineers can already run. The paid value has to come from the requirements and remediation layer.

Platform bundling by chip and OS vendors: silicon and RTOS vendors (Arm's PSA Certified framework, secure-element and TrustZone SDKs, Mocana-style embedded security stacks) are building security requirements and certification into the platform the maker already buys. That pre-empts the requirements taxonomy at its source and threatens the planned chip-vendor channel, which depends on partners who may prefer their own scheme.
objections.evidence: https://www.psacertified.org/ (chip-ecosystem certification with certified-product database); concept:go_to_market.channel (partnerships with chip vendors)

objections.objection: The runtime on-device protection feature puts the product up against Karamba, Mocana and similar embedded runtime vendors, which have head starts. It spreads a 25-person team across a fifth front and confuses positioning against the analysis and certification incumbents.
objections.evidence: concept:mvp.features (Lightweight on-device protection added post-deployment); concept:competitors[Karamba Security, Mocana]

strongest_point: No incumbent combines automated firmware analysis with device-specific, implementable requirements and remediation guidance for makers who have no product-security team. Labs are manual and SCA tools stop at CVE lists.
what_would_change_my_mind: A large carrier, retailer or distributor agreeing to accept or require the startup's certification in its supplier onboarding
Head-to-head pilots where the requirement and remediation output closes findings faster than a Synopsys binary scan plus a UL engagement, for 3 of 5 makers
A partnership in which a recognised lab or standards body uses the platform as its automated pre-assessment, which turns the most dangerous competitor into a channel
